Flying scientists into the heart of fire-generated thunderstorms might sound like the plot of a disaster movie – but this daring mission is happening in real life.

It’s part of NASA’s INSPYRE project, which aims to unravel the mysteries of pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCbs), or ‘fire clouds’.

The barely studied phenomenon has been seen this summer in wildfires raging in the US, and for the first time ever in France.

PyroCbs spew volcanic-scale plumes of smoke and particles 50,000 feet into the air. They hamper firefighting and are so powerful that they can cook up their own thunderstorms – including lightning strikes that spark new blazes.

They also loft smoke high into the stratosphere where it can linger for upwards of a year, impacting weather, climate and the Earth’s protective ozone layer.

For the next six weeks, NASA pilots will chase wildfires from airbases in Colorado and Montana.

Scientists on board the planes will gather data which they hope will help predict where and how pyroCbs form, as well as measure their effect on climate. Findings are expected within a year.

Image: NASA

Food banks saved a whopping half a million tonnes of food from going to waste in 2025, as partnerships with farmers and retailers spared wonky fruit and vegetables from landfill.

The Global FoodBanking Network (GFN) says the saving stopped around two million tonnes of CO2 from entering the atmosphere, equivalent to taking 473,000 cars off the road for a year.

However, the news might be seen as a double-edged sword, as GFN food banks fed 2.5 million more people last year than in 2024. That amounts to two billion meals served to 40.5 million people and, the organisation suggests, is an indicator of increasing hunger amid aid cuts, rising prices and geopolitical crises.

“Food banks – ever agile, responsive and resilient – continued to serve as safety nets around the world, connecting local communities to nutritious food, despite the challenges,” said GFN president Lisa Moon.

Images: Sameoldsmith

The EU has greenlit a breakthrough eye implant that can help restore vision for those suffering from one of the most common age-related causes of vision loss.

The PRIMA implant employs hundreds of pixels which stimulate retinal cells by converting light signals beamed from a special pair of glasses. The gizmo even has a zoom-in feature to magnify tiny text.

The innovation comes from US-based Science Corporation and aims to manage the effects of age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

The condition, which primarily impacts people aged over 50, causes blurry or missing central vision, impacting daily tasks like reading, driving and recognising faces.

In clinical trials, PRIMA improved vision for 80% of patients. The device has now gained CE (Conformité Européenne) certification under EU medical device regulations, making it potentially available across 30 European countries.

Mahi Muqit, a vitreoretinal consultant at London’s Moorfields Eye Hospital, which led the UK arm of the trial, commented: “Blind patients are actually able to have meaningful central vision restoration, which has never been done before.”

Image: PRIMA

Twelve of the animals were moved 106km (65 miles) from their home in Murchison Falls National Park to Ajai Wildlife Reserve.

Betsy Robertson was standing in the center of the Spokane Convention Center on Monday afternoon, but she wasn’t there for a gala or a conference. Instead, the event space in the middle of Washington state’s second-largest city had been transformed into a Red Cross emergency shelter as a trio of wildfires, just a few miles away, burned down entire neighborhoods.

Nurses and volunteers were moving between the rows of cots around Robertson, making sure that the hundreds of evacuees—from the mothers with their babies to the elderly with their caretakers—had blankets and enough to eat. Just outside, the air was noxious with smoke “thick enough to burn your eyes,” she said.

Robertson, a communications director for the Red Cross, is from Washington and has been with the organization for 10 years. She has seen communities devastated by wildfires before. But never like this.

“The scale of homes destroyed and lives changed forever—this is a new level,” she said. “We are bracing ourselves for seasons like this getting worse and worse, and starting earlier and going later.”

A historically dry winter, extreme drought, and heat waves set the stage for the hundreds of wildfires that have burned across the Pacific Northwest this summer. Dozens of large ones have broken out in the past week alone. Though it’s still early in the fire season, Oregon recently broke its annual record for acreage burned with nearly 2 million acres scorched.

Washington is also in the middle of its most destructive season on record, with more than half a million acres burned and at least 65,000 residents ordered to evacuate across the state. The three large fires that started on Saturday around Spokane had destroyed more than 700 buildings by Monday afternoon.

“I’ve been trying to wrap my mind around how we’re going to house all these folks,” said Kitty Klitzke, a member of the Spokane City Council representing a hard-hit area where two fires were burning on Tuesday morning. Many of the people displaced by the fires in Spokane are senior citizens and their caretakers. “It’s a miracle that, so far, we know of no fatalities and no reported missing people,” Klitzke said.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Did you know that every time the brain learns something, it changes physically? A study in PLoS Biology is the first to track exactly what those changes are, and found two separate processes happening at different speeds and in different locations, and that the tool most researchers have been […]

Actual Article Body:

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Did you know that every time the brain learns something, it changes physically? A study in PLoS Biology is the first to track exactly what those changes are, and found two separate processes happening at different speeds and in different locations, and that the tool most researchers have been using couldn’t tell them apart.

Standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tracks water movement through brain tissue but collapses everything into one signal. “DTI captures a single, global signal: it can tell you that a change in one region lasts longer than in another, but not what underlies it,” said Valeria Della-Maggiore, who led the study from the National University of San Martin and the University of Buenos Aires. Her team used ultra-high-gradient MRI combined with a model called SANDI (Soma and Neurite Density Imaging), which separates the signal by cellular compartment: cell bodies, neurites, and surrounding fluid.

Twenty-nine healthy adults, ages 18 to 36, learned a five-digit finger-tapping sequence with their non-dominant left hand. They practiced 15 blocks of 12 sequences with 25-second rests between blocks, about 15 to 20 minutes total. Scans were taken before the session, 30 minutes after, and 24 hours later.

The 30-minute scans showed a temporary rise in cell body density across all brain regions involved in the task: the hippocampus, primary motor cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and precuneus. By 24 hours, those had returned to baseline. The researchers interpret this as a housekeeping response: intense neural activity disrupts the ion balance in cells, water flows in to compensate, and the cells swell temporarily.

The second change was more specific. At 24 hours, neurite density (dendrites and axons) had increased in just two regions: the precuneus and the posterior parietal cortex. The change held, and it correlated with how much each person improved. The hippocampus, engaged early in learning, showed no lasting structural change at all. Whatever long-term rewiring happened, it happened in the cortex.

“When you learn a new skill, two processes of different spatial and temporal dynamics take place in your brain at the cellular level,” Della-Maggiore said. “One is transient and occurs at the level of cell bodies. The other is persistent, confined to the regions specifically involved in learning.”

Standard DTI would have read both as one. The temporary swelling would have disappeared into the noise.

Della-Maggiore said the SANDI method could extend to studying neurodegeneration, aging, and development, anywhere the difference between adaptive change and damage matters and can’t currently be measured directly in living humans.

Source study: PLoS Biology– Learning engages transient and sustained cellular mechanisms in the human brain

Actual Article Body:

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Here’s some food for thought: for students, free lunch ends when school does. For the millions of children who rely on subsidized cafeteria meals during the year, nothing automatically fills that gap in June. On July 1, Governor Kathy Hochul announced that $189 million in Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer funds had already reached nearly 1.6 million low-income children across the state, with roughly $240 million projected to reach around 2 million kids before the season is out.

A USDA demonstration project found that summer food benefits cut the share of children experiencing very low food security by one-third. Summer hunger doesn’t get much coverage. That number suggests it probably should.

Each eligible child gets $120 on an EBT card that works like SNAP at authorized grocery stores and farmers markets. Families already enrolled in SNAP, Public Assistance, or Medicaid get it automatically, with no application. Families not automatically enrolled have until September 8, 2026 to apply online at ny.gov/SummerEBT.

Important to note: the $120 expires 122 days after it’s issued, and any unused balance disappears once that window closes. Families should use it soon after the card arrives. To qualify, a child must attend a school that participates in the National School Lunch Program and meet the income thresholds for free or reduced-price meals.

Joel Berg, CEO of Hunger Free America, named the core problem: children who get school meals during the year “don’t receive government-funded food at summer meals sites when schools are closed.” Richard R. Buery Jr., CEO of Robin Hood, described summer as a time when “school meals disappear and budgets are stretched thin” for low-income families across the state. Both were making the same basic point: the gap is structural, and it opens every year on the same date.

The EBT spending also moves through neighborhoods. No Kid Hungry New York Director Rachel Sabella noted that the dollars “strengthen local economies by allowing recipients to spend them at neighborhood grocery stores, farmers markets, and other local businesses.” Assemblymember Maritza Davila, chair of the Assembly Social Services Committee, described families already “struggling with the rising cost of everything in their lives from housing, medical care and especially food costs,” with summer adding more weight to that load.

Federal nutrition programs are facing Republican-backed cuts in Congress. Senator Charles Schumer called federal funding for hungry children “more critical than ever,” citing reductions he said are already taking effect. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who pushed to make the federal Summer EBT program permanent, described New York’s program as a direct response to that federal retreat.

New York’s FY27 budget went well beyond the EBT rollout. Hochul secured $51 million for the Hunger Prevention and Nutrition Assistance Program, $15 million to expand it to regional food banks and pantries, and $55 million for the Nourish NY program, plus $395 million to continue Universal Free School Meals through fiscal year 2027. Kate Breslin of the Schuyler Center for Analysis and Advocacy cited a Federal Reserve Bank of New York finding of “a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among households with young children.” Families who haven’t received their benefits yet have until September 8, 2026, to apply.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Czech researchers at the University of Chemistry and Technology in Prague are building titanium joint implants with a porous internal structure designed to hold medication and release it gradually after surgery. Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Czech researchers at the University of Chemistry and Technology in Prague are building titanium joint implants with a porous internal structure designed to hold medication and release it gradually after surgery. The project is a collaboration with surgeons at Motol University Hospital.

The implants use laser powder bed fusion: a thin layer of titanium powder is spread, a laser fuses it into shape, and the process repeats roughly 1,300 times for a knee implant. The full print takes about ten and a half hours. Researcher Jiří Kubásek calls the machine “extremely precise,” capable of recreating the microscopic architecture of actual bone.

“Bone tissue isn’t solid. It’s naturally porous, which allows body fluids to circulate through it,” Kubásek said. “The pores are only tens to hundreds of micrometers wide, and this printer allows us to recreate structures of exactly that scale.”

Porous implants bond better with surrounding bone because tissue can grow into the gaps. But the pores also work as drug reservoirs. One version in testing uses a carrier of sulfates, phosphates, and silver, with the antibiotic vancomycin mixed in, to ward off post-operative infection.

Professor Dalibor Vojtěch, who leads part of the project, says the main technical problem is finding a carrier material that is safe for the body and breaks down at a controlled rate. The medication has to release gradually, not in one dose. The team hasn’t solved that yet, but they’ve already demonstrated implants for the hip, shoulder, and ankle.

Post-operative infection is one of the worst complications of joint replacement. Loading preventive medication directly into the implant, rather than relying on systemic antibiotics, is what the whole project is really about.

How inherited genetics shape the way cancer forms and evolves

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A study published in Nature provides the first experimental evidence that inherited genetics shape not just whether cancer starts, but how it evolves once it does. Researchers led by Duncan Odom at the CRUK Cambridge Institute exposed four genetically distinct strains of mice to identical doses of diethylnitrosamine, a […]
The post How inherited genetics shape the way cancer forms and evolves first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.

Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

A study published in Nature provides the first experimental evidence that inherited genetics shape not just whether cancer starts, but how it evolves once it does.

Researchers led by Duncan Odom at the CRUK Cambridge Institute exposed four genetically distinct strains of mice to identical doses of diethylnitrosamine, a liver carcinogen found in tobacco smoke and some processed foods. All four groups got the same dose at the same age, 15 days old. Nearly 600 tumors were then analyzed to trace how each cancer had developed.

Cancers in the different strains took different genetic routes. Most tumors ended up activating the same cancer-promoting biological processes, but they reached that point through different mutations and genetic changes. The genetic variation between strains was relatively modest, comparable to the genetic diversity found in human populations, and yet the differences in tumor evolution were substantial.

Sarah Aitken, an Assistant Professor at Yale School of Medicine who worked on the study at the CRUK Cambridge Institute, said the findings matter for both screening and drug selection. “How people respond to cancer drugs is likely to differ depending on their inherited genetics, and so we may need to tailor our diagnostics and treatments accordingly,” she said. The team also suggests this extends to how patients respond to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

“We’ve been able to show for the first time the extent to which genetic background influences both the mutation processes and the pathways leading to tumor development,” said Odom, who now leads research at the German Cancer Research Centre in Heidelberg. Sam Godfrey, Cancer Research UK’s research information lead, called it a “fascinating hint” that inherited genes “might have a big influence on the way that cancers develop after DNA damage.”

The study was in mice. Whether and how the findings translate to humans remain open questions. What they do suggest is that cancer screening built around shared environmental risks may not be accounting for the full picture of who develops cancer, and why.

Source study: Nature–Genetic background sets the trajectory of experimental cancer evolution

A brush fire jumped over the 5 Freeway after igniting in Gorman on Friday afternoon, prompting evacuation orders, lane closures and heavy traffic delays through the Grapevine.

The blaze, dubbed the Ridge fire, was reported around 3 p.m. near the 39000 block of Gorman Post Road and quickly burned about 100 acres of surrounding brush in northwestern Los Angeles County.

Less than three hours later, the fire had grown to 1,000 acres, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

Around 4:45 p.m., the fire crossed the 5, leading authorities to issue an evacuation order in areas of Gorman and Hungry Valley west of the freeway. Evacuation warnings are also in place to the south and north of the blaze, as well as in the adjacent area of Kern County.

A map of areas affected by evacuations can be found here.

The 5 Freeway was initially closed in both directions around the fire, snarling rush hour traffic. Southbound lanes reopened shortly before 7 p.m., while northbound lanes reopened around 9 p.m., according to the California Highway Patrol.

The South Coast Air Quality Management District issued a smoke advisory for portions of northern L.A. County, which will be in effect until 2 p.m. Saturday. Residents who can see or smell smoke are advised to remain indoors with their doors and windows closed, an air purifier running and air conditioning turned off.

The L.A. County Fire Department has deployed around 230 firefighters, according to department spokesperson Jonathan Torres. At one point, a total of 11 aerial resources, including fixed-wing aircraft and firefighting helicopters, were assigned to the incident.

The fire’s rapid initial growth was fueled by south-to-southeast winds of 6 to 10 mph, with gusts of up to 15 mph, according to the National Weather Service. Temperatures in the area were in the lower 90s, and humidity levels were about 18% around the time of ignition.

The toasty temperatures and steep, brushy terrain initially led the fire to spread quickly, according to Torres. However, firefighters were able to gain ground as temperatures cooled into the evening.

“It’s not as hot as it was at the start, so the conditions did become favorable for us,” he said around 6 p.m. “I know we’re making very good progress.”

Additional crews and resources from the Ventura County Fire Department, Kern County Fire Department and Angeles National Forest are also helping to combat the blaze. At least three helicopters will remain assigned to the incident after dark and continue to perform water drops, Torres said.

Actual Article Body:
People have long saved for life's biggest milestones: buying a home, getting married, and retirement. Some workers are also putting money aside for something they hope never happens: burnout.

Last week, Mary Kane handed in her resignation letter.

After six months of feeling exhausted, irritable, and increasingly burned out in her job as a senior marketing manager, the 54-year-old Minnesotan decided she'd had enough.

Unlike many workers in a similar position, she wasn't terrified about how she'd pay the bills once she quit. For years, she says, she saved about half of every paycheck, building what she now calls a burnout fund.

A burnout fund is a ring-fenced savings pot designed to fund a recovery period, rather than unexpected emergencies such as job loss or medical bills.

"A burnout fund is really intentional savings where you anticipate needing to take a break," Julie Beckham, Rockland Trust's financial education and development strategy officer, told Business Insider.

In that sense, she added, it's an old concept under a new name: "Being intentional in naming any savings account is a good practice."

Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.

Sabino Vargas, senior financial advisor at Vanguard, told Business Insider the goal with a burnout fund is to "build enough financial flexibility so you can have choices if a step back or career reset is needed."

Has burnout affected how you spend or save your money? We'd love to hear your story. Contact this reporter at jzitser@businessinsider.com.

The concept of the burnout fund is entering the conversation as a series of workplace and economic pressures are taking their toll on workers in different ways. AI is accelerating the pace of work, shaking people's sense of job security, and leaving many workers feeling perpetually in catch-up mode. Rising prices have many feeling financially strapped. On top of that, the US job market is looking increasingly rocky. The BLS reported Friday that the US lost 23,000 jobs in July, and revisions to previous reports meant 100,000 fewer jobs were added in the previous two months than originally thought.

Several surveys suggest that burnout is widespread. A National Alliance on Mental Illness-Ipsos Workplace Mental Health poll of 2,153 full-time employees at companies with more than 100 workers, conducted in January and February, found that 53% felt burned out because of their jobs. It's affecting employees at every level; a recent string of high-profile tech execs and founders cited health issues and burnout as reasons for stepping back from their jobs.

While the World Health Organization doesn't classify burnout as a medical condition, it recognizes it as an "occupational phenomenon" resulting from chronic workplace stress.

Tasmin Lofthouse, 33, first burned out in 2018. "I was completely flat, no get-up-and-go. I didn't want to do anything, see friends, or speak to them," the marketing professional, based in northwest England, told Business Insider.

Lofthouse knew she needed to leave her job, but with no savings, she couldn't afford to. Instead, she left for another job almost immediately after quitting.

She launched a marketing consultancy in 2020 and experienced another period of burnout two years later. This time, she decided she never wanted money to dictate whether she could step away from work. "It made me realize I needed to build some sort of avenue to allow me to step back when I'm burning out," she said.

Lofthouse started saving money in 2022 and opened a dedicated burnout fund in 2024. Since then, she has transferred part of her business profits into it every few months. Now she has around £48,000 ($65,000) set aside, enough to cover 12 months of business expenses while paying herself a reduced salary. She also maintains a separate emergency fund covering three months of living expenses.

Actual Article Body:
Kazakhstan has taken a massive step towards its long-held goal of re-establishing the tiger in the country by releasing a female Amur tiger into the Ile-Balkhash Nature Reserve.

Established in 2018 for this exact purpose, what followed was a truly generational effort of reforestation and replenishing prey species of deer and antelope that the Caspian tiger, now extinct, once relied on.

“Today, we witnessed a truly historic event,” Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Yerlan Nyssanbayev said at the ceremony which saw the female tiger named “hope” in the Kazakh language, leap from the container on the back of a truck into the reserve.

“For the first time since the tiger disappeared from Kazakhstan more than 70 years ago, the first tiger has been released into its historical range. This is the result of many years of work by the state, our Russian colleagues, scientists, and international partners,” he said.

The extinct Caspian tiger, also called the Turanian tiger, was most closely related to the Siberian, or Amur, tiger, and so Russian collaboration was essential to the project.

In 2020, Bukhara deer were re-established in the reserve, before the saiga antelope, and the Asiatic wild ass, or kulan, followed.

Before they could roam as their extinct cousins did, hope and 3 other tigers: a male named Amur and two cubs brought from Russia’s Khabarovsk Reserve were released into large enclosures to adapt to the sights, smells, sounds, and weather.

Hope was examined by veterinarians and determined to be in sterling condition, She was fitted with a GPS tracking collar and, driven out into the reserve, allowed to go her own way.

The male, Amur, remains in captivity as experts monitor his behavior to determine whether he will be capable of hunting in this new environment.

The cubs will grow up semi-wild in the reserve, with the intent to release them when they’re fully mature, or around 18 months of age, provided they pass behavioral assessments for hunting and survival instincts. This slow, gradual approach, Astana Times wrote, reflects the complexity of introducing large predators to new landscapes.

Part of that complexity involves the safety and security of the communities surrounding Ile-Balkhash. Though large, the reserve is not fenced, allowing tigers to spill out back into their ancestral environment as their populations grow.

“The safety of people living near the reserve is our top priority,” officials from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Ecology said. “We’ve put measures in place to prevent conflicts between people and tigers, including a dedicated team that will respond if an animal approaches a populated area.”

If the program succeeds, Kazakhstan will become the world’s first country to re-establish the tiger into an ecosystem it had disappeared from.

Actual Article Body:
Scientists using Earth’s most powerful solar telescope have snapped a picture of the Sun’s surface that helped explain—for the first time—foundational physics about our dear star.

Situated atop the summit of Haleakalā, a volcano on the island of Maui, the Daniel Inouye Solar Telescope peered down onto the surface of the Sun. Captured in the data is proof that the plasma thereupon is subjected to the same physical force that causes waves to break and whirlpools to form down on Earth’s seas, or among Jupiter’s clouds.

Published in the journal Nature, the authors of a paper on the discovery said it carries “far-reaching implications for our understanding of the creation and dissipation of magnetic fields,” on the Sun’s photosphere.

“The vortex formation on the Sun has long been a central question in solar physics. For the first time, we have identified both their origin and their driving mechanism,” lead study author Dr. David Kuridze, assistant astronomer at the National Solar Observatory in Boulder, Colorado, wrote to CNN in an email.

The phenomenon is known as Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability.

“Although theoretical models had suggested that the right conditions for Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability could exist in the photosphere, seeing these structures widespread across the surface was still a huge surprise.”

The discovery promises a wealth of further information on the mechanics of solar flares and coronal mass ejections, phenomena which, when occurring in the direction of Earth, can interfere with satellite communications and power grids, cause the Northern and Southern lights, and even destroy electrical equipment.

It also could help scientists understand why the Sun’s outer atmosphere is hotter than its surface.

Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability occurs when two fluids moving at different speeds pass each other in different directions. The perturbations caused by the interaction form vortices. The images from the Inouye telescope mark the first time the phenomenon has been seen on the Sun.

Kuridze later told CNN to think of the vortices as small engines that drive magnetism, energy, and heat up from the surface to the Sun’s outer atmosphere. This occurs, in part, through flux braiding, another potential signature of the vortices.

The vortices have the power to intertwine lines of a magnetic field, which generate heat when they snap and reform. For their research, the scientists pointed the Inouye Telescope at a magnetically-active area next to a large Sunspot.

CNN reported that the general consensus in solar physics is that these small solar whirlpools are far more relevant to the formation and expression of massive and rare solar events than other signs in the lead up to those events.

The ultimate reward of this work would be the ability to interpret the formation and movements of the vortices as signs of future, larger events that could potentially affect Earth.

Starting the Van Kannel Revolving Door Company in 1889, his idea was so successful that he was eventually bought out by the International Steel Company which created amphibious landing vehicles for battle tanks for World War II. However, the only remaining vestiges of that company is, in fact, its revolving door division.

This simple invention, when laid out by Van Kannel in his patent submission, really becomes quite brilliant. It possesses, he wrote, “numerous advantages over a hinged-door structure … it is perfectly noiseless … effectually prevents the entrance of wind, snow, rain or dust … Moreover, the door cannot be blown open by the wind … there is no possibility of collision, and yet persons can pass both in and out at the same time.”

A year after his patent submission, in 1889, the Franklin Institute of Philadelphia awarded the John Scott Legacy Medal for it, but Van Kannel would have to wait another ten years before the first revolving door was installed at Rector’s, a restaurant on Times Square in Manhattan. (1888)

“These plants have been used in different forms of medicine throughout the world for thousands of years,” said MSU alum Garret Miller, co-first author of the paper and now an assistant professor of biotechnology at University of Michigan-Flint.

“We know they interreact with our bodies in so many ways, and understanding how to create them can help provide totally new routes of testing.”

“Plants are the best chemists around, upgrading their arsenal of natural compounds over millions of years to help them survive,” said Björn Hamberger, study author an Endowed Professor in MSU’s Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology.

At MSU, the Hamberger Lab explores these diverse compounds, better known as specialized metabolites, and how they can be leveraged for the greater good. History has shown they’re more than capable of the opposite, with wolfsbane possibly at the seen of multiple historic assassinations, including Socrates, Alexander of Macedon, and Cleopatra’s sister.

In more recent years his team had set their sights on larkspur—also called delphinium for its dolphin-shaped flowers—wanting to know exactly how the plant produced a mix of toxic-yet-promising chemicals known as diterpenoid alkaloids.

Diterpenoid alkaloids are the intersection of the two oldest and largest classes of plant chemicals on the planet, and researchers have faced an uphill battle to determine their mind-bendingly complex structures.

The two labs decided to join forces, before beginning the task of identifying the exact chemical pathway the two plants took to produce their diterpenoid alkaloids.

Because plants naturally produce specialized metabolites slowly and in tiny amounts, discovering these pathways is a vital step toward engineering plant chemistries that can tackle real-world, large-scale challenges.

From the beginning, Plaid Cymru was stuck between Labor, the Liberals, and the Tories, arguing that the greatest share possible of Welsh rule should be reserved for Welsh people. From there they have steadily grown in support to be able to contest, and eventually win elections.

To a Mouse includes the famous line “The best laid plans of mice and men oft go awry.” In the poem about Maggy the mare, he opens in his classic rhyming pattern, this one in Scotts:

A Guid New-year I wish thee, Maggie!
Hae, there’s a ripp to thy auld baggie:
Tho’ thou’s howe-backit now, an’ knaggie,
I’ve seen the day
Thou could hae gaen like ony staggie,
Out-owre the lay.

In it, he notes a louse crawling on a lady’s bonnet in church, and at first, chastises the insect for its misconduct, but then realizes that to a louse, all humans must seem the same, and that if only human and louse could see each other through each other’s eyes, they would understand one another. An alternative interpretation is that the poet is musing to himself how horrified and humbled the pious woman would be if she were aware she was harboring a common parasite in her hair.

Oh, would some Power give us the gift
To see ourselves as others see us!
It would from many a blunder free us,
And foolish notion:
What airs in dress and gait would leave us,

OpenAI said Friday it has suspended work on some aspects of its upcoming model Astra after an internal review found it had made significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity — enough to warrant concern over its capabilities.

OpenAI said in a blog post Friday that this model, which is still in development, reached its “critical cybersecurity threshold,” meaning it could independently identify and carry out cyberattacks against traditionally well-protected real-world systems. Under the company’s “Preparedness Framework,” which it created in 2023, this triggered additional safeguards.

“While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out Critical capability level at this time,” OpenAI wrote. “Astra is an upcoming model, and was not involved in exploiting Hugging Face.”

The disclosure highlights an unusual moment in the topsy-turvy and still nascent frontier AI labs sector. Companies across every industry hold back products over potential risks, including for safety and cybersecurity concerns. But they rarely announce those decisions publicly when it’s a product that is still under development.

In this case, OpenAI is already under scrutiny after a different unreleased model breached Hugging Face’s systems during internal testing — the first verifiable incident of an AI lab losing control of its model. Since then, OpenAI and AI labs such as Anthropic have disclosed other incidents in which AI models breached their sandboxes and posed threats during cybersecurity tests.

The string of cases — seems like a new disclosure every day now — has triggered varying reactions from cybersecurity experts, lawmakers, and the AI labs themselves. Some express fear and call for stricter oversight. But there’s also a bit of flexing. In certain circles, any AI lab with a model that has that kind of capability will be seen as an impressive advancement.

OpenAI said it was sharing this information because it believes “it’s important to be transparent with the public and the safety and security communities about this potential shift in capabilities.”

The AI lab said it’s also taking action, including enacting stricter security controls and pausing internal activities involving Astra that don’t meet these beefed guardrails. OpenAI said it is working with relevant government agencies and “select AI safety organizations” to test the capabilities for this model.

Cloudflare is the latest company to join the race to build a new web browser. But instead of pitching a Chrome alternative to consumers, the internet infrastructure provider launched Kitesurf, a cloud-hosted browser designed specifically for AI agents.

AI software is evolving from chatbots that answer questions to agents that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. Browsers are a critical part of this transition, as they’ll need to navigate the web and use websites, as humans do.

Unlike traditional web browsers built for humans, a browser built for AI agents doesn’t care about visual elements, like themes, tabs, or browser extensions, Cloudflare explained in its announcement. A browser designed for AI agents needs to manage context windows, performance, token costs, and scalability. It also faces a different threat model because an AI browser could be subject to vulnerabilities like prompt injection attacks and more, the company noted.

With Kitesurf, AI developers will be able to build software that can navigate websites, fill out forms, and complete other browser-based tasks, without having to build their own browser software.

Cloudflare says it decided to build Kitesurf just 12 weeks ago, and it runs entirely on top of the company’s serverless platform, called Workers. Kitesurf is available for free while in beta in Browser Run, which lets developers programmatically control and interact with headless browser instances on Cloudflare’s network.

For developers, Cloudflare’s pitch is that this enables AI agents to use the web more efficiently while using less computing power than Chromium, which keeps costs down.

“Kitesurf is significantly more efficient in CPU and memory consumption than Chromium for common agentic tasks like screenshots and HTML extraction,” according to the company.

The browser itself was built from other technologies, including a modular rendering engine from Blitz; Firefox’s CSS parser, Stylo; and Boa JS, a Rust ECMAScript engine. Everything else runs inside Cloudflare Workers. Although still new, Cloudflare says Kitesurf already passes around 215,000+ web platform tests, and it’s adding hundreds more, passing tests every week.

Cloudflare also credited the open source Rust headless engine, Obscura, for inspiring it to develop Kitesurf, noting that the first proof of concept was a port of Obscura to Workers.

The company said the browser correctly renders pages like TodoMVC, a popular benchmark application for comparing JavaScript frameworks, along with Wikipedia, Hacker News, the Cloudflare Blog, and much of the Cloudflare dashboard.

Kimi K3, the latest AI model made by Chinese company Moonshot, escaped an environment set up to test its cyber capabilities, researchers said in a blog post published on Friday.

The news shows once again that companies and independent organizations are struggling to contain their AI models designed for hacking.

The U.S. job market unexpectedly stalled in July.

A report Friday from the Labor Department shows that employers cut 23,000 jobs last month, and job gains for May and June were revised sharply lower.

The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%, but only because more than 260,000 people dropped out of the workforce.

It was the second month in a row that the monthly jobs tally came in weaker than forecasters had expected.

"We are increasingly hearing from workers that they are anxious about their job security and they are frustrated by the fact that they are stuck in roles that are not necessarily good for them," said Daniel Zhao, chief economist at the job search website Glassdoor. "And that's on top of workers who are not in a job right now and feel frozen out of the job market."

Glassdoor's worker confidence index slumped in July to a record low.

Restaurants and retailers cut thousands of jobs last month, and local government also saw large job losses. Healthcare continued to add workers, but at a more modest pace than earlier in the year.

The softening job market may complicate the Federal Reserve's job, since it's also battling stubborn inflation. The Fed may be more cautious about raising interest rates at a time when the labor market appears less stable.

For people who are working, average wages have risen 3.2% in the last 12 months. That's likely not enough to keep pace with inflation, however, so workers' paychecks don't stretch as far as they used to.

"Part of the reason that workers are feeling bad about today's job market," Zhao says, is that "a lot of those wage gains have been eaten up by rising energy prices."

AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond has apologised for his part in Geelong's controversial concussion contract with defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

Drummond was Geelong president two years ago when premiership defender Kolodjashnij signed a contract in which he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

It is understood Kolodjashnij's agent was not aware of the contract, and neither the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) or AFL were informed at the time.

It is also understood that while Kolodjashnij passed an independent medical test, he was still considered at risk of future complications from head injuries.

Jake's twin brother, Kade, was forced to retire from the game in 2020 due to ongoing concussion problems.

"I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024," Drummond said.

"This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board.

"Jake's welfare was central to all discussions, and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days.

Geelong is finally issued a 'please explain' over its controversial concussion contract with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

"While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.

"Regardless of the player's agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed."

Drummond said it was an error to keep the process quiet, and clarified that he would not be involved in AFL discussions about the matter.

"As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA," Drummond said.

"I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations.

"I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation."

Speaking to ABC Sport ahead of the Saturday games, AFL boss Andrew Dillon reiterated that it was a complex situation.

"This is an issue that is really complex and in this one in particular it's complex and unique," Dillon said.

"But concussion and the effects that has on players or participants in contact sports ... is an issue that's confronting contact sports worldwide.

"What we have here is a player that has suffered multiple concussions, went before an AFL concussion panel, ultimately over a period of months was cleared as fit to play.

"Through that period, over a number of months, Jake's worked with the club doctors, independent medical experts, the club, and the club board and management to make sure that he understood their were risks to continue playing, not withstanding that you've been cleared medically fit to play.

"That was the intent behind what was going on."

Dillon said the please explain was around why the concussion agreement sat alongside his playing contract.

"We've gone to Geelong under the rules and asked them why it wasn't lodged with us," Dillon said.

"So we're waiting to hear back from Geelong on that."

The Cats are expected to be fined over the contract saga after initially being cleared of wrongdoing.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

Penrith captain Isaah Yeo may miss the rest of the NRL season after injuring his pectoral muscle, while the Sydney Roosters joined the Panthers on top of the table after defeating the Canterbury Bulldogs.

Yeo came off in the first half of Penrith's 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland on Friday night, with the Auckland-based side solidifying their status as a genuine premiership threat in 2026.

Yeo was clutching his pectoral muscle after reeling out of a tackle, with scans needed to confirm if he has sustained a tear.

Should scans confirm a pectoral tear, he could be out for the rest of the season.

"It doesn't look great," Panthers coach Ivan Cleary said during his press conference.

"Obviously Yeoy's a big loss and hard to replace, but that's how it goes.

"If that's the case, we'll have to (replace him)."

The Roosters have joined the Panthers on 36 points at the top of the NRL ladder, surviving a scare to pip the Bulldogs 20-18.

The Roosters held an 8-2 lead at half-time, but the Bulldogs scored three tries in 11 minutes to take an 18-8 lead with 25 minutes to play.

But two quick tries in the final 15 minutes for the Roosters earned them a hard-fought win.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.

Australia's Alex de Minaur has let a big opportunity slip at the Canadian Open, losing to Britain's Cameron Norrie after holding match point.

De Minaur was third seed at the Open, also known as the Montreal Masters, but he threw in two key double faults to give up the lead and lose to Norrie 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1.

De Minaur can only drop from seven to eight in the world rankings if Ben Shelton wins the title, which means the Aussie will keep his top-eight seeding for the US Open.

A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

Four members of the Ugandan boxing team and one member of the Pakistani boxing team have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games.

Scottish police are investigating the reports and engaging with the Home Office.

Uganda's chef de mission said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Luke Beveridge says he would have signed a contract as a player to continue his career in spite of concussions. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
